{"docket_number": "72-734", "additional_docket_numbers": null, "term": "1973", "first_party": "United States", "first_party_label": "Petitioner", "second_party": "John P. Calandra", "second_party_label": "Respondent", "manner_of_jurisdiction": "Writ of certiorari", "lower_court": "United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit", "argued": ["1973-10-11T05:00:00Z"], "question": "

Can a witness refuse to answer questions before a grand jury when the questions are based on evidence obtained during a search that the witness feels is unlawful?

", "facts_of_the_case": "

A federal grand jury questioned John P. Calandra in connection with loan sharking activities. The questions were based on evidence obtained during a search of Calandra’s business, Royal Machine and Tool Company. Calandra refused to answer any questions, arguing that the search of Royal Machine unlawfully violated the Fourth Amendment. The government attempted to grant Calandra immunity in district court, but he asked the court to suppress evidence obtained during the search. The district court granted the suppression order and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed, holding that the Fourth Amendment exclusionary rule applied. Under the exclusionary rule, any evidence obtained during an unlawful search and seizure cannot be used against the victim of that search in a criminal proceeding.

", "conclusion": "

No. Justice Lewis F. Powell, writing for a 6-3 majority, reversed the lower court. The Supreme Court held that the exclusionary rule does not apply in grand jury proceedings. The purpose of a grand jury is to determine whether a crime was committed and whether to charge someone in connection with that crime. Using the exclusionary rule would interfere with that purpose. The exclusionary rule is also meant to deter police misconduct, not provide a new constitutional right.

Justice William J. Brennan dissented, writing that application of the exclusionary rule should not depend on whether it deters police misconduct. The exclusionary rule gives meaning to the Fourth Amendments protection against unlawful search and seizure. Justice William O. Douglas and Justice Thurgood Marshall joined the dissent.

analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Mr. Rottetower, you may continue. Mr. Chief Justice, please the Court. I think I should digress for a moment and speak briefly about the fundamental difference in the Fourth Amendment versus the Fifth Amendment. Reaching so as to ultimately reach the question of whether or not the grant of immunity in the facts of this case resolves to a great extent a great part of the case. Of course, I don't believe that it does. The Fifth Amendment fundamentally, briefly, in effect states that an individual shall not be forced to be a witness against himself. If he is not going to be prosecuted, if the sovereign says to the witness, we are not going to prosecute you for anything about which you testify, then there's no possibility that that individual can be a witness against himself. Therefore, he must answer the questions. On the other hand, the Fourth Amendment protects privacy, the right to personal security, in effect. And the Fourth Amendment right of privacy applies regardless of whether you are in a criminal setting, whether there's a possibility of criminal prosecution, or whether there's a possibility of self-incrimination. That's irrelevant. I think that's the teaching of this Court in Camarera, where we're dealing with health inspection ordinances. And the Court says it's anomalous for us to say that Fourth Amendment rights depend upon prospective criminal proceedings or the possibility of self-incrimination. So, therefore, we're going to be down the road on the violation of privacy by the time you get to where this problem arose. In this case, Mr. Chief Justice? Well, I guess that's what the government means when they talk about immediacy of the Fourth Amendment violation. Time-wise, from the original violation of the facts in this case, we are some months away. But the question asked in the grand jury, albeit some months away from the original intrusion, considerably Fourth Amendment violation, is in itself, according to a respondent, a separate, distinct violation of the Fourth Amendment, which springs from another Fourth Amendment violation which occurred months prior. This is something like, I suppose, the concept of exclusion by the way of the fruits doctrine, is it not? Well, I prefer not to get into the question of whether this is an exclusionary rule concept or not. Because that's the question raised by the petition for certiorari. So we have to get into it. That's what the government has framed this case. And they'd like the court to believe that we're talking about a furtherance of the exclusionary rule. But the respondent does not agree. It's the respondent's position that we're talking about additional violations of the Fourth Amendment or new violations springing from prior violations but not necessarily exclusion. What the court is doing... Yes, it has nuances, as Justice Stewart suggested, nuances, which perhaps is also true of the fruit doctrine. Is it not so? Yes, it does. You can view it. It depends upon whether you look at exclusion. I look at exclusion as a remedy as opposed to a right. And I believe what we're all involved in here is the prevention of a right violation. What case of this court describes the exclusionary rule as a remedy in the sense you're using a remedy for the party? I think the entire map versus Ohio really talks about how do we restore this individual or how do we restore this individual to a point where the violation is remedied. I don't recall any case in which the court has ever discussed any concept except the broad range of keeping the system, the integrity of the system protected from the use of illegally acquired evidence, not as any benefit for the individual but as for the benefit of the system. Isn't that the rationale underlying the exclusionary doctrine? Certainly that is the basic rationale. They don't do it because of any right on the part of the defendant who's asserting it. Yes, they do it in the sense that what is involved, if the evidence is allowed to be introduced in the criminal proceeding, is we bring about in effect a combination of Fourth and Fifth Amendment violations which in effect bring about a disruption of the system, an infection of the legal system. Haven't some of the cases simply said that the defendant in a case where the exclusionary doctrine is applied is merely an incidental and often an undeserving beneficiary? Yes. Language something to that. There has been language to that effect, Mr. Chief Justice, and certainly it's on the basis that this will deter further violations. Can you think of any case in which a defendant who succeeded in suppressing evidence was deserving in the sense that he had earned it in some way? Well, I think if we talk in terms of Silverthorne, certainly... Papers, as distinguished from heroin, for example. I really don't think we can't place a condition on the Fourth Amendment depending upon the subject matter of the search, which is in question. Well, you wouldn't suggest that a man who's found with 10,000 pounds or whatever it may be of heroin concealed in the back of a truck deserves anything from society or from the courts? I think he deserves the full protection of the Constitution. Deserving in the sense that he personally deserves what flows from the exclusionary doctrine. Isn't it the system that the courts were trying to protect? Yes. The integrity of the system, the integrity of the truth-seeking process. Right. And also to deter future violations. No, the deterrence was a very major factor, wasn't it? But we're not involved in that type of situation here. We're talking about here the district court initially deciding whether or not it's going to protect or prevent ongoing, immediate violations of the Fourth Amendment by the questions. And the court has a right to do that because we have circuit court opinions which tell us that an individual who can prove that Fourth Amendment or Fifth Amendment violations are ongoing and continuing has a right to get them enjoined by the federal court. The Fourth Amendment is not in the system. No, it isn't in this case. Mr. Justice Powell and I mean Mr. Justice Marshall. I have great problems on the Fourth Amendment in this context without the Fifth. Well. As I mentioned this morning. Yes, I know, and that's why I started out my argument after the luncheon recess by getting back to the fundamental differences. I think, for example, if we look at Camara, the health inspection ordinance situation, if the state and Camara told Camara that you are not going to be prosecuted at all and nothing we find will be used against you, but just let us come in and inspect your building, this court would arrive at the same decision that it arrived at because we're talking about the right, his right to be free from that intrusion. And there's no possibility of self-incrimination. There's no possibility of criminal prosecution. But yet there's the Fourth Amendment right to be secure in his privacy. And I think that's the fundamental interest that the district court wanted to prevent a violation of when it ordered the prosecutors not to ask any questions. Once again, is there any distinction between a trial and the grand jury on that point? In this situation, no. The respondent would have to take the position that if these facts arose at trial, the decision must be the same. Well, you're caught in my horse and different. My point was assuming that it would be wrong at a trial as if necessarily wrong in the grand jury. Well, yes and no. If we think in terms of the exclusionary rule, we know a defendant himself, a prospective defendant, the person that the grand jury is going to indict, does not have a right to suppress that evidence. But this isn't a person with the grand jury. But he'd have the right to raise it at trial, of course. This man is not going to be indict. No. No, he isn't. And you don't see any difference? No, I don't. Because whether the question is asked of him in the grand jury or whether the questions are asked of him in the trial, in either setting, they amount to an intrusion into his privacy, an area protected by the Fourth Amendment. And if the prosecutor should ask him in his office, it would be the same thing. Yes, that's correct. In your theory. Yes. I think... I have great trouble with the case that says that. Silvertone didn't say that. Well, I don't think there's been any case that says it directly. Yeah. But certainly, Mr... The Court of Appeals in this case said it. The Court of Appeals in this case said it. And I think Mr. Justice Douglas said it in Galbard, in effect. This case was, I see, decided before this Court's decision in Galbard, was it not? I noticed that the... The Court of Appeals decision? Yeah. Yes, it was. It cites Galbard and its companion cases indicating that certiorari was granted. Yes, it was. That's correct. And I believe the government, after Galbard, petitioned for reconsideration by the Sixth Circuit. The Sixth Circuit denied reconsideration in view of Galbard. I think a moment must be given to the policy consideration of a rule to the contrary of the rule announced in this case by the Sixth Circuit and the District Court. And I think that brings right to the fore Mr. Douglas's, Mr. Justice Douglas's comments in Galbard and also the district, the chief judge of the District Court's comment in this case and the Sixth Circuit's comment. And that is a rule different from the result below in this case would supply police with an added incentive to violate the rights of suspected co-conspirators in order to marshal evidence against alleged ringleaders. Now, before that statement, which is a paraphrase of Mr. Justice Douglas's statement in Galbard, the chief judge of the District Court said in effect the same thing and the Circuit Court of Appeals unanimously made the same observation. And for those reasons, we respectfully request that this court affirm the Sixth Circuit and the District Court's opinions. Thank you, Mr. Auditari. Mr. Clayborne? Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the Court. In light of some of the questions explored by the Chief Justice and Mr. Justice Stewart and Mr. Justice White, I think it may be useful to make a further comment on this proposition that each question of this witness is a further separate, distinct invasion of his right of privacy guaranteed by the Fourth Amendment. I find it extraordinary that that should be treated as the stronger side of Respondent's case. If he were arguing that the very record seized illegally ought not be used even before the grand jury, Silverthorne might give him some support. Here we are well beyond that. We are not talking about the exclusion of the seized records. We are talking about the fruit of a poison tree attenuated further down the line. We are talking about material that wasn't obtained directly by any illegal action on the part of the government. We are talking about evidence that would normally be available to the government, however intrusive it might be on the witness, however unpleasant it might be for him to testify, his normal obligation as a witness before a grand jury or a trial would be to divulge this relevant information which the government is seeking of him. Would they have known about it had they not carried out the illegal search? Perfect. It is conceded, Mr. Justice White, that they would not have known about it. But at least we are not talking about the very immediate fruit. Isn't that normally what we talk about? If you happen to learn something from an illegal search, that's fruits even though if you had known about it before, you might have been able to get a warrant. I'm not suggesting, Mr. Justice White, that this isn't covered by the fruit of the poisonous tree doctrine. I am suggesting that there is no further separate distinct invasion of Fourth Amendment rights. If the exclusionary rule as applied to poisonous fruits were to bar the use of this evidence because it is derivative from an illegal act... No, but they've got to get additional information. Yes, but only the prophylactic deterrent value of the exclusionary rule would justify depriving the public at trial of this information. What if one of the questions was now, we learn from these papers, we seize that you have another paper at home. Now, just please turn that over. I would have supposed that, and so far as we're talking about either an immunized witness at trial or a proceeding before the grand jury, the government would be free to subpoena that additional paper. Although there is a further invasion there of the same kind. But that subpoena would have... is not an invasion of the Fourth Amendment in itself. That subpoena would have been wholly proper. Yeah, your argument would be very interesting and very persuasive were it not for the Silverthorne case. Well, Mr. Justice Stewart, I've attempted to distinguish the Silverthorne case. I think it is fair to say that the Silverthorne case, because it arose after the man had been indicted, and therefore was really an effort to exclude from trial, not from the grand jury, evidence which would have been useful. The grand jury had already seen these records seized in Silverthorne. The man had already been indicted. They used the grand jury process to obtain the same records through subpoena. However, it wasn't to produce them before the grand jury. It was obviously to produce them at trial. But it was a contempt. It was in a... Well, but the contempt, it should have been done in the 17th. Silverthorne wasn't a reversal of any conviction. There hadn't been any trial. Quite right, Mr. Justice Stewart. But it was a block to an attempt to use records for a forthcoming trial. It was a premature attempt. You concede everything Silverthorne held by conceding that they could have the records back and keep them. In this case. In this case. That's correct. But beyond that, I must say that if... What did you do? There may have been a question in Silverthorne, and one doesn't know how broad the ruling was, as to whether the photographs of the records would have been usable at trial. It wasn't held, was it? Well, the opinion, as we know, contains language so broad that it would seem to bar... That's sort of the issue here, isn't it? But this court has long since repudiated the broad dictum of Silverthorne, if only an alderman, by saying the Fourth Amendment does not mean that illegally seized evidence may not be used at all. On the contrary, it may be used against someone not the victim. For instance, it may be used by way of impeachment. Those would be seemingly barred uses under the broadest interpretation of Silverthorne. Is it under Silverthorne, isn't the potential for disruption of an ongoing grand jury investigation more limited than would be involved here, too, since there had already been a separate determination of illegality? Quite true. And also, Mr. Justice Rehnquist, since the indictment had already been returned, there was no disruption of the grand jury proceeding. The grand jury had finished its work. We were simply prematurely barring evidence from trial, or the court was. It should have been done when it was sought to be introduced rather than when the subpoena was served. But that's, as the court viewed it, a difference without constitutional importance. But it was plainly barring the government from using the illegally seized evidence at trial. And to that extent is, of course, and has always been invoked by this court, as the first extension of weeks of the exclusionary rule to reach a second attempt, or a derivative attempt, to exploit an illegal activity. As I repeat here, the nexus between the illegality and the testimony sought to be obtained is remote. It is, therefore, less offensive, less of a violation of the exclusionary rule, than it would be if the very records involved were sought to be used. What's the difference between putting in a record which shows that I loan-shocked you, Joe Doakes, out of $100, and asking you, isn't it true that you loan-shocked Joe out of $100? The difference is what? I would suppose, Mr. Justice Marshall, that in the second case, if the answer were yes, there could be no argument about it, whereas the record might be ambiguous. It might supply something which the paper itself did not. This may not be that situation, but we must assume that the government was seeking to get more than it already had through the record. Well, assuming that you can't put in the record, then you can answer the question. You can ask the question. But if the question is exactly what's in the record, what is the difference as to that man's rights? Well, I may have misled the court somewhat by conceding that a motion to return the property would be available. It doesn't follow, in my view, that the government would not be free to use copies before the grand jury. The reason for the rule of return is that a man is entitled, if it's lawful property and not contraband, to its return when it's been obtained in an improper way. It doesn't either follow that a subsequent subpoena wouldn't reach it. The Silverthorne says no. But, again, not in the context, really, of a grand jury proceeding, but rather in the context of a forthcoming trial. We would, if Bush, take the position that it would be proper to obtain at least copies of the material itself that had been improperly seized in the first instance. The invasion having been not enriching that material, which was in no sense privileged, but in the way in which it was obtained by an intrusive search, also the court held, without justification, without sufficient probable cause. But the material isn't privileged. It's very unlike the presidential tapes with respect to which a privilege may exist in no matter what custody, in no matter what method is attempted to be used to obtain them, or a lawyer's work papers, or a doctor's records of his patient, which can't be reached either by search or by subpoena. Here we're talking about material that is not privileged, that could be reached by subpoena. The only flaw was that it was reached at the first time by a procedure which was unduly intrusive. But it was that intrusion that violated the Fourth Amendment, not the obtaining of the paper, which could legitimately be obtained, and the obtaining of which would in no conceivable way violate the Fourth Amendment had it been done by subpoena. You submitted and there replied that Silverthorne was wrongly decided. We say, Mr. Justice Stewart, that if the distinctions we attempt to draw are not accepted, and if pushed that far, we would take that view. Understanding it only as holding that a subpoena couldn't reach these papers on the ground that they'd somehow been immunized because at one time they'd been wrongly seized. With that submission, we pray that the judgment below be reversed. Thank you, Mr. Claiborne, and thank you, Mr. Rotetari. The case is submitted.
